summary: Presents extensions to RSVP for generic policy-based admission control, letting policy information be carried along with reservation requests. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: It adds a note field to reservation requests so the rules about who may reserve can travel with them.

subtitle: How RSVP carries policy information in POLICY_DATA objects so admission control can consider more than free bandwidth.

tldr.problem: RSVP gives some users better service than others, yet the base RSVP admission control looks only at resource availability, with no standard way to carry access or usage policy.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2750 defines the format of the POLICY_DATA object and its options, rules for how RSVP nodes forward, refresh, expire and report errors on policy data, and an optional INTEGRITY object for policy nodes that are not neighbors.
tldr.outcome: RSVP messages can carry opaque policy elements between policy-capable nodes, even across nodes that know nothing about policy. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2205.

today: RFC 2750 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2000. It updates RFC 2205, and the unit data lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why RSVP Needs Policy Control
sections.content:
RSVP by definition discriminates between users by giving some better service at the expense of others, so it is reasonable to expect mechanisms that control and enforce access and usage policies. Version 1 of the RSVP functional specification left a placeholder for this: the POLICY_DATA object. Its admission control interface, however, is based only on resource availability.

RFC 2750 describes extensions for policy based admission control. Its scope is limited to the extensions; it does not advocate a specific architecture for policy based controls. A router and policy server protocol for these extensions is described in other RFCs, including COPS (RFC 2748) and COPS usage for RSVP (RFC 2749). The document treats a Policy Decision Point (PDP) as including a Local Decision Point.
sections.eli5: A line for a ride at a fair should let some people in and keep others out based on rules. This RFC adds a way to write those rules on the ticket.

sections.title: A Simple Scenario: PEPs and PINs
sections.content:
The RFC assumes policy enforcement will first concentrate on border nodes between autonomous systems. Its example domain has two boundary nodes (A and C) that act as policy enforcement points controlled by PDPs, and a core node (B) in between. Node B is a policy ignorant node (PIN): it can process RSVP messages, but it is not trusted to handle policy information.

Policy objects cross the domain by passing through the PIN. The document describes processing rules for both enforcement nodes and PIN nodes.
sections.eli5: Two guards stand at the doors of a building and check the rules. The hallway in between has people who pass notes along but are not trusted to read or change them.

sections.title: The POLICY_DATA Object
sections.content:
POLICY_DATA objects ride inside RSVP messages. Any policy-capable node can generate, modify or remove them, even when senders and receivers do not provide them and may not know they exist. Exchanging them between policy-capable nodes along the data path supports consistent end-to-end policy, including across administrative domains when border nodes translate objects under bilateral agreements.

The object is class 14, C-Type 1. After the usual length and class fields come a 16-bit Data Offset, giving the offset in bytes of the data portion from the first byte of the object header, and a 16-bit reserved field that is always 0. These are followed by an option list and a policy element list.

Policy elements have a length, a P-Type and opaque policy information. Their contents are opaque to RSVP and are understood only by policy peers such as a PDP.
sections.eli5: The object is an envelope with a small label on the front saying where the contents start. Inside are optional extras and the actual rules, which only the right office can read.

sections.title: Options Inside POLICY_DATA
sections.content:
All options are RSVP objects whose meaning is adjusted when used as policy data options.

  • FILTER_SPEC list or SCOPE: names the senders the policy applies to. If neither is present, the policy covers all flows of the session. The two are mutually exclusive. The SCOPE option helps prevent policy loops but may greatly affect the size of the object.
  • Originating RSVP_HOP: identifies the policy-capable peer that built the object, which may be several RSVP hops away. If absent, the sender named in the RSVP message is assumed.
  • Destination RSVP_HOP: a second RSVP_HOP that names the target policy node. A node SHOULD ignore policy data whose destination does not match its own IP address. The RFC notes this can help prevent replay of a policy object elsewhere.
  • INTEGRITY: lets non-neighboring policy nodes secure policy data without involving the PINs in between.
  • Policy Refresh TIME_VALUES (PRT): slows policy refreshes when policy has looser timing needs than RSVP.

For PRT, the minimal value is R, and lower values are treated as R. A multiplier is computed as N=Floor(PRT/R), giving a policy refresh period of R'=N*R, so refresh and cleanup are both slowed by a factor of N. It applies to no-change periodic refreshes only; a route change forces an immediate update. A weak certificate can be sent with every refresh and a strong certificate less often.
sections.eli5: The envelope can have optional stickers. One lists who the rule is about, one says who wrote it and who it is for, one is a tamper seal, and one says how often to repeat the reminder.

sections.title: State, Forwarding and Errors
sections.content:
Policy state expires per policy element, because POLICY_DATA objects are only containers. Elements expire at the same time as the RSVP state received in the same message, except that PRT controlled state expires N times slower. Only one element of a given P-Type can be active at a time, so a new one from the same PDP replaces the old one. An empty element of a P-Type deletes all policy state of that type.

The memo mandates policy control for Path, Resv, PathErr and ResvErr messages only. PathTear and ResvTear are exempt, because integrity verification makes sure a Tear comes from the node that installed the reservation, and a Tear is equivalent to withholding refreshes.

A PIN MUST forward received POLICY_DATA objects unmodified. At multicast merge points it should concatenate multiple objects from downstream when sending upstream, and copy a single object from upstream to all downstream branches.

Policy errors are reported in ResvErr or PathErr messages with a policy failure code in the ERROR_SPEC object, and the error message must include a POLICY_DATA object with the details. For a failed multicast reservation, RSVP should deliver the policy ResvErr to all downstream hops and let the PDP decide where it goes, rather than looking for the culprit as it does for Blockade State.
sections.eli5: Notes expire when the reservation does, and a new note of the same kind replaces the old one. Middle stops pass notes along untouched, and if something goes wrong the answer comes back with an explanation.

sections.title: Policy Error Codes
sections.content:
Appendix A extends the RSVP error list. It defines Error Code 02, Policy Control failure, in the ERROR_SPEC object (class 6), with a 16-bit error value. Values include generic rejection, quota or accounting violation, preemption, expiry of an unrefreshed policy, a failed integrity check and a PDP that is down.

Values between 2^15 and 2^16-1 are available for site or vendor use. Errors specific to a policy element are carried back inside a POLICY_DATA object, while the RSVP error code gives a simple, less secure way to report generic policy errors. The two are likely to be used together.
sections.eli5: When a request is turned down, the reply carries a number saying why. Examples are over the limit, kicked out by someone more important, or the rule-keeper is not answering.

sections.title: Integrity and Security
sections.content:
Two optional mechanisms protect the integrity of policy data. The first uses RSVP integrity (RFC 2747) to build a chain of trust when every RSVP node is policy capable. The second uses the INTEGRITY object inside POLICY_DATA to protect data between non-neighboring policy enforcement points, which matters when PINs are trusted for RSVP signaling but not for policy.

Appendix B explains the computation. The digest is calculated over the POLICY_DATA object with a copy of the RSVP SESSION object temporarily appended, with the SESSION flags set to 0. The PDP chooses the key and hash algorithm. The appended session is not kept as part of the object, and the remaining steps follow RFC 2747.
sections.eli5: A sealed stamp on the note lets the two guards check that nobody in the hallway changed it, even though the hallway passed it along.

sections.title: IANA Registry for Policy Elements
sections.content: IANA keeps a registry of RSVP policy elements, identified by P-Type. Numbers 0-49151 are standard policy elements allocated by IETF Consensus. Numbers 49152-53247 are vendor specific, one per vendor, allocated first come first served. Numbers 53248-65535 are reserved for private use and are not assigned by IANA.
sections.eli5: Every kind of rule note gets a number. Some numbers are for official kinds, some are handed out to companies, and some are left free for anyone to use privately.
